what_it_does: Genome assembly — reconstructing a complete DNA sequence from millions of short fragments — requires enormous amounts of RAM (over 500 GB just for 10% of the human genome) and is so memory-starved that the processor sits idle most of the time waiting for data. NMP-PaK solves this by placing small custom processors directly inside the memory module itself, so data barely has to move at all, and by cleverly batching the work to slash peak memory usage. The result is 16x faster than a high-end CPU and 8.3x more throughput per machine than a supercomputer cluster, while using a fraction of the power and chip area.
method_in_detail:
The idea. Genome assembly works by breaking DNA into 32-character snippets called k-mers, building a graph where each node (called a MacroNode) groups related snippets, and then repeatedly compacting that graph until long contiguous sequences emerge. The compaction step — where nodes are merged and their bookkeeping information (called TransferNodes) is handed to neighbors — dominates 48% of total runtime. The processor spends 54% of that time just waiting for data to arrive from RAM, and uses only 2.5% of the available memory bandwidth, meaning the memory bus is almost entirely idle.

How it works. NMP-PaK places custom processing units (PEs, small circuits that do simple integer arithmetic) directly inside the buffer chip that sits between the memory bus and the RAM chips on a standard memory stick (called a DIMM). This is called channel-level near-memory processing — the compute sits at the memory channel, not in the CPU. Because the PEs live right next to the data, they can read many MacroNodes simultaneously, jumping memory bandwidth utilization from 2.5% to 44%. Each PE runs a three-stage pipeline: first it checks whether a node should be merged (Stage P1, the Invalidation Check); then it pulls out the transfer package for that node (Stage P2, TransferNode Extraction); finally it routes and applies that package to the destination node (Stage P3, Routing and Update). A crossbar switch inside the DIMM routes packages between PEs on the same stick, and a network bridge handles cross-DIMM traffic.

The key design choice. Most MacroNodes are small (under 1 KB), but a tiny fraction grow huge. Instead of making the PEs big enough to handle the giants — which would waste chip area — NMP-PaK simply sends anything over 1 KB back to the CPU. Because these large nodes are so rare, the CPU finishes while the PEs are still working, hiding the cost entirely.

The other catch: memory. Even with fast in-memory processing, 10% of the human genome needs 528 GB of RAM. NMP-PaK solves this with batch processing — it divides the genome into 10% chunks, assembles each one separately (requiring only ~379 GB), then merges the tiny compacted results at the end. This cuts peak memory 14x with no meaningful loss in output quality.

The result. Against a CPU baseline: 16x faster overall. Against a GPU: 5.7x faster, because GPUs choke on the fine-grained irregular memory reads. Against a supercomputer with 16,384 CPU cores: 8.3x more genomes assembled per machine per hour, using 385x less power and 293x less chip area.
